title: Dynamical backaction in nanoscale superfluid electromechanics
authors: Marek Talíř, Filip Novotný, Balázs Szalai, Nasiruddin Mondal, Emil Varga
abstract: Nanofluidic acoustic resonators employing superfluid $^4$He can be used to study quantized vortices from collective behavior in two-dimensional superfluid turbulence down to few individual vortices created by rotation. In order to improve sensitivity to the level needed for probing individual quantized vortices, readout mechanisms employing optomechanical or optomechanics-inspired approaches seem to be promising in this regard. In this work, we develop an electromechanical system, which couples a 4$^\mathrm{th}$ sound acoustic resonance to a superconducting LC tank circuit in a sideband-resolved regime. Using this system, we demonstrate electromechanically induced transparency (EMIT), optical spring effect and optomechanical sideband damping and amplification. Furthermore, by rotating the cryostat, we demonstrate sensitivity to quantized vortices, which can become trapped and released in avalanche-like process inside the nanofluidic volume.
summary: This paper details the development of a highly sensitive electromechanical resonator coupled to superfluid helium to study quantized vortices. By utilizing techniques like Electromechanically Induced Transparency, the authors measure the damping induced by vortices ($\Gamma_L$), demonstrating that this dissipation is history-dependent and can be manipulated through controlled thermal or mechanical pulsing.
main_problem: The study aims to improve the sensitivity of detecting quantized vortices in superfluid helium by coupling the acoustic resonance to an electromechanical readout system.
main_result: The system successfully demonstrates electromechanically induced transparency and measures vortex-induced damping ($\Gamma_L$), showing that this damping is history-dependent and can be controlled via annealing pulses.
method: The research combines theoretical modeling (FEM, circuit analysis) with advanced experimental techniques like Electromechanically Induced Transparency/Absorption (EMIT/A) to probe dissipation.
model_or_system: The platform is a nanofluidic acoustic resonator etched into $	ext{SiO}_2$, operating in superfluid Helium-4, whose acoustic mode is coupled to a superconducting LC tank circuit. The coupling allows for the study of superfluid dynamics, including vortex motion.
key_observables: Vortex-induced damping ($\Gamma_L$), linewidth ($\Gamma_M$), EMIT/A spectra, and the rate of change of dissipation with rotation history.
important_parameters: LC resonance frequency ($\omega_C$), acoustic mode frequencies ($\Omega_M$), zero-point fluctuation amplitude ($	ext{y}_{	ext{ZPF}}$), and the mutual friction constant ($\hat{\alpha}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling the system in the sideband-resolved regime and assumes that measured damping can be separated into intrinsic, backaction, and vortex-related components.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physical setup, FEM simulations of acoustic modes, EMIT/A spectra demonstrating backaction, and time-series plots showing $\Gamma_L$ evolution during rotation ramps and annealing.
paper_structure: The work progresses from establishing the physical electromechanical coupling and demonstrating backaction effects (EMIT/A) to quantifying the vortex-induced damping ($\Gamma_L$) by measuring the deviation from the backaction-modified linewidth, culminating in studies of the history-dependent nature of vortex dissipation.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it merges quantum optics (EMIT/A, cavity coupling) with superfluid physics (quantized vortices), providing a sensitive, controllable quantum sensor platform for studying non-equilibrium many-body phenomena.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The nanofluidic Helmholtz resonator. a) Photograph of the resonator. Green colour is due to thin- film optical interference and outlines the nanofluidic cavity. b) Atomic force micrograph of the electrode edge inside the basin. c) Schematic view of the resonator dimensions, electrodes in gray. Electrode thickness is approximately 60 nm, cavity height quartz-to-quartz 900 nm.

Figure 2: Resonance of the LC tank circuit. a) Normalized transmission of LC resonance with increasing probe amplitude, showing nonlinearity and Q degradation above 0.5 V. b) The circuit diagram for measuring the LC resonance.

Figure 3: Acoustic modes inside the Helmholtz resonator. a) Finite element simulation of acoustic pressure profile for the first three visible modes. The bending of SiO2 substrate is simulated alongside pressure acous- tics in a coupled 3D geometry (the COMSOL ”multiphysics” coupling). b) Superfluid velocity calculated from the same simulation. c) Experimentally observed resonances using EMIT, with detuning ∆= 0 in order to observe the intrinsic mechanical linewidth. The signal from lock-in amplifier is offset to zero and normalized to 1 on resonance. See Tab. 1 for calculated properties of the acoustic modes.

Figure 4: Electromechanically induced transparency and absorption. a) EMIT (red) and EMIA (blue) measurement of the coupled system. b) Zoom to acoustic peak on LC resonance. The x-axis is |ωd −ωp|/2π. c) Circuit diagram for measuring EMIT/A, the strong drive signal from G2 is added to weaker probe signal from G1 (which is measured using a lock-in amplifier). d) Relation of drive and probe frequencies to ωLC and ΩM.
